key_concept: Potash alum is the double salt $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot 24H_2O$, i.e. $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot 12H_2O$, so ion ratios come straight from its formula.
steps: Write the formula of potash alum: $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot 24H_2O$.
Count the ions in this formula: $K^+ = 2$, $Al^{3+} = 2$ and $SO_4^{2-} = 1 + 3 = 4$.
Check with the simplest formula $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot 12H_2O$: it has 1 $K^+$ and 2 $SO_4^{2-}$, giving $1:2$.
Check charge balance: $(+1) + (+3) + 2(-2) = 0$, so the formula is consistent.
why_not_others: $2:1$ inverts the ratio. $2:3$ and $3:2$ come from counting the sulphates of only $K_2SO_4$ or only $Al_2(SO_4)_3$ instead of adding both $(1 + 3 = 4)$.
common_trap: Forgetting to add the sulphate from $K_2SO_4$ to the three sulphates from $Al_2(SO_4)_3$, or reading the ratio in reverse order.
time_saving_tip: Memorise alum as $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot 12H_2O$. The ratio $K^+ : Al^{3+} : SO_4^{2-} = 1:1:2$ can then be read off directly.
